title: MAJESTIC!
reviewNotes: Four branches begin after Kxc6 at 43s, with White Ka6/Bg5/c2/d2 against Kc6/a3/d4. Bf6/Kd5/d3/a2/c4 checks both en passant and Kc5 defenses. Quiet Kb7 turns a1=Q into actual Be7 mate; an independent king retreat allows Bxd4. Premature Bxd4 loses the bishop and the exact ending. This is a closely related version of Most Majestic Game (zpX6pvMJhto), whose bishop starts on h4 rather than g5; both reach the same Bf6 core. The earlier eight-piece knight sacrifice remains context. The later caption A3 is corrected to the visually supported d3.

Instead, he plays D3. [music] This doesn't seem to create any threats. The pawn simply goes to A2. But as it turns out, there was an idea behind A3 to prepare the move C4. This is a check, so black has to reply. And the first thing that might come to mind is to take this pawn with en passant. But actually, if black does that, now the bishop is all of a sudden free to capture this pawn and it's going to prevent the promotion. And look at the harmony between the pawn and the bishop preventing the king [music] from coming to capture this pawn. But so what? Black doesn't have to take en passant. He can simply go to C5 and still [music] defend the D4 pawn. And now again, white seems simply lost. Except he [music] isn't. Because in this position, white plays one of the most amazing moves I've ever seen. The only winning move in this position is the incredible the majestic and beautifully counterintuitive [music] king to B7. White, cool, calm, and collected, takes one step with the king.
